about: The city's calendar and memory (urbs_town.gd): the week and its market day, the festivals of a short year, what happens at set hours (processions, a speech from the Rostra, the crier), rain, what people say to each other, gossip, favours, the sounds of the trades, and the regulars you come to know across the ages. {a} and {b} are two people's names, {other} and {title} someone you have met.

festivals.name: the Saturnalia
festivals.news: It's the Saturnalia! No work, gifts, dice in the street, and the slaves sit at table with their masters. Io Saturnalia!
cries: A gift for you, a candle, cheap!

festivals.name: the Lupercalia
festivals.news: The Lupercalia! The young men run round the Palatine in goatskins and strike the women with thongs, for luck with children.

festivals.name: the Parilia, Rome's birthday
festivals.news: The Parilia today: Rome's birthday. Bonfires tonight, and the shepherds leap over them.

festivals.name: the Roman Games
festivals.news: The Roman Games! Races in the Circus all week. The whole city's going.

festivals.name: Easter
festivals.news: Easter. Christ is risen. The new Christians are baptised tonight, all in white.

cries: A white ox for the god!

republic: Citizens! The grain must come before the games!
Who will stand for the people, if not I?
The Senate is the Republic!
empire: Citizens! The Emperor's generosity feeds us all!
Praise to the Senate and the Roman people!
late: The city has its walls and its bread. Be grateful!
The Emperor, far away, thinks of Rome!

republic: Auction at the Temple of Castor! A house on the Carinae!
Lost! A slave boy, Syrian, answers to Eros!
empire: Games at the Amphitheatre, the Kalends! Fifty pairs of gladiators!
Auction! Wine from Campania, a hundred jars!
late: By order of the Prefect: bread at the steps at the ninth hour!
Races at the Circus! Greens against Blues!

republic: It's market day! The country's come to town!
Chickens! Eggs! Cheese from Tusculum!
empire: Market day! Everything from the farms!
Honey! Fresh honey!
late: Market day, what there is of it.
Beans, cheap!
Bread for the poor, one each!
God bless the bishop!
fall: Bread from the Pope's farms! One loaf each!

chatter: Salve, {b}! Busy?
Always, {a}. You?
Did you hear about the fire on the Esquiline?
Three floors. The landlord was asleep in Tibur, of course.
{b}, you still owe me for the figs.
Tomorrow, {a}, tomorrow.
Hot today.
Hotter up on the fifth floor, believe me.
How's the wife, {b}?
Louder than ever, {a}, thank you.
Going to the baths?
After the eighth hour. Save me a place.
The price of oil!
Don't start me, {a}. Don't start me.
Who's giving the games this year?
Some aedile with more money than sense. Thank the gods.
Your boy's grown, {b}.
Eats like a legion, {a}.
Seen the new shrine at the crossroads?
Fresh paint and all. The neighbourhood paid.
gossip: You met {other}? The {title}? Keep an eye on your purse, that's all I'll say.
{other} the {title}? Owes half the street money. Charming, though.
Oh, {other}. The {title}. Their {kin} ran off with a Greek, did you know?
{other} the {title} is saving to buy a shop of their own. Good luck to them.
If {other} the {title} says prices are going up, they're going up. They always know.

asks: Do me a kindness, stranger. Tell {target}, the {title}, that {msg}. They'll know what it means.
If you pass {target} the {title}, tell them {msg}. I can't leave the shop.
messages: the wife wants them home for dinner
thanks: {from} sent you? Thank the gods. Tell them I'll be round.
Ha! From {from}? Good news. Here, you're a friend now.
after: You told {target}? You're a good sort, stranger.
Thanks for the message. They came by.

republic: Felix, baker, like my father. This oven's been going since before Hannibal. Well, near enough.
My girl's to be married at the Kalends. I'm baking the cake myself, and it'll be the best in Rome.
The wedding was grand. She cried, I cried, the donkeys cried. Now who's going to keep my accounts?
empire: Numisius Felix. Four generations in this bakery. My great-grandfather baked the cake for his own daughter's wedding here.
The state buys our bread for the dole now. Steady money. The Felixes have never had it so good.
We've put the family name on the lintel in marble. Let them remember us.
late: Numisia. I run the bakery now: my husband's dead and my brothers took the guild posts. Bread's baked bread, whoever bakes it.
The guild of bakers is bound to the trade now, by law. Our children must be bakers too. Well. It's a living.
The old marble over the door says Felix. Nobody remembers who he was.
fall: See that doorway? There was a bakery there, they say. The Felixes. Bread for the whole street, once.
No flour, no oven, no Felixes. The Goths took the last of the grain.
Spare a crust, stranger? For the old baker's sake.

republic: Hilarus. Twelve fights, twelve alive. Three more and I get the wooden sword.
Fourteen now. The crowd shouted my name. One more, stranger. One more.
Free! The wooden sword, see? I'm going to open a tavern. You'll come.
empire: Callistus. Net and trident. The crowd loves a retiarius, and the murmillones hate us.
Hilarus's Tavern, down the Subura? My grandfather drank there. Some freed Thracian started it.
Twenty-one fights. The emperor himself nodded to me. Nodded!
late: Nicias. I fought, when there were fights worth the name. Constantine doesn't like the games. The bishops don't either.
Now I teach young fools to hold a sword for the beast hunts. It's not the same.
When I'm gone, who'll remember how it was done?

republic: Caecilius Rufus. That theatre of Pompey's is a disgrace. A temple on top so it can't be pulled down! Clever. Disgraceful.
My son went to the theatre. My son! Next he'll be wearing Greek slippers.
Very well, I went. The seats are comfortable. Tell no one.
empire: Caecilius Rufus. My family has sat in the Senate since the Republic. We used to decide things. Now we agree beautifully.
My ancestor refused to set foot in Pompey's theatre. I have a box in it.
The emperor asked my advice today. I gave it. He did the opposite. We all smiled.
late: Caecilius Rufus. My family keeps the old gods, at home, quietly. Jupiter has been good to the Caecilii for five hundred years.
The emperor lives in the east. The bishop lives in the Lateran. We live in our libraries.
When I die, my grandson will be baptised. I know it. I shan't watch.
fall: Caecilius Rufus. Of the Senate. Such as it is. Totila took half of us to Campania as hostages.
My house on the Caelian has no roof now. We live by the river like everyone.
Six hundred years of Caecilii. I may be the last one who remembers the name meant something.

republic: Fabia. Fish. My mother sold fish on this bank and so will my daughters, if I can keep them off the boats.
The mullet are running. Rich men's cooks fight over them. I let them.
My eldest has a fisherman. Very handsome. Smells like me.
empire: Fabia. Fish, like all the Fabiae on this bank since forever.
Oysters from Lake Lucrinus now. The rich eat them by the hundred. I sell them by the hundred.
The bridge downstream's new. Still the same river.
late: Fabia Maria. I was baptised last Easter, but I still pour a bit of wine for the river god. Just in case.
Fish on Fridays now, for the Christians. Business has never been better.
The river's older than any god. I'll keep them both happy.
fall: Maria. The river feeds us now that the aqueducts are cut. Fish and water, that's Rome.
The mill boats scare the fish. But bread is bread.
My grandmother's grandmother sold fish right here. The river doesn't care who rules.

republic: Stephanus. Sit! You'll hear everything worth hearing in this chair, and some things that aren't.
Did you hear? The aedile's wife and the gladiator. No? Sit down, sit down.
You're a regular now, stranger. Regulars get the good gossip and the sharp razor.
empire: Stephanus, like my father and his father. The chair's the same. Mind the crack.
Everyone wants a beard like the emperor's now. Hadrian did that. Ruined barbers for a generation.
You again! You look like you need a trim and a story.
late: Stephanus. Same chair, same crack, four hundred years. Well, I tell people four hundred.
The monks want their heads shaved on top. Easy money. They don't tip.
Stay a while. There aren't so many to talk to as there were.
